In fact, the PSA test sometimes presents erroneous results, with false negative or even false positive results, leading to unnecessary medical interventions.
It is more than enough reason to make men, already reluctant in themselves, doubt whether they should have the detection tests.
To take the test or not?
We have consulted two specialists.
In studies conducted in the United States, a high rate of contagion was detected among sample groups, making it difficult to interpret those data and make firm recommendations.
The European study showed some difference in mortality between patients who had undergone detection and those who had not.
The study, with a 12-year follow-up, also showed that there is between a 30 and 40% chance of developing metastases if the detection test has not been done.
I therefore recommend the test from the age of 50, or from the age of 40 if your father has had prostate cancer.
African-American men have a higher risk index.
The key is to make a good decision once cancer is detected.
There are aggressive cancers and others that are indolent.

It is truly necessary to ensure that the patient understands the degree of risk of his cancer. All possible options should be offered to him, and not necessarily treat prostate cancers that do not threaten long-term life, in which case active disease monitoring should be chosen instead.

Instead, we suggest active monitoring of the disease and, if it progresses, we offer them treatment.
We are increasingly determining precise criteria to decide who should or should not be treated.
I recommend that the test is done in any case.

Palliative care. The best way to die... | Le Devoir
In its Commission to Die with Dignity, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of the end of life.
The debate must be resumed soon while a bill is being prepared.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still much to do.
Le Devoir has tried to get close to it.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. was living alone in his apartment in the Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him two years of relief.

"They had given me five years of life, but I've already lived seven," he says, a fact that he has become a pass, lying on his bed in the Victor-Gadbois palliative care center in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has caused him great weakness: a huge weakness that prevents him from going to the bathroom alone and even from eating on his own.
Sitting in front of an appetizing lunch, he accepts resignedly that they will help him eat.
Brave, he even smiles, talks to strangers who pay him attention, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The bravery of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a remedy for that illness.
"Throughout our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois center.
Returning to one's childhood, for certain people, is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he states.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients entering the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses surrounding them no longer offer "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., 89 years old, is to die "conscious and drowned".
But the illness has made him discover his children.
"I have good children," he adds.
"I no longer have any desires in this life," he says, before accepting that a mask will be placed on him to help him breathe.
And he is expecting, in the coming days, a final visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, the care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
They are palliative care that are given when nothing else can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have a palliative care bed for every 11,700 inhabitants.
It's very little, since we know that we will all eventually die one day.
Here, life continues in the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the center.
Whether at the level of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual.
The dying man is given mouth wash with brandy or Pepsi, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their sugar levels.
Death is part of everyday life.
Last night we served a beer to Mr. X, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both the patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
At the Victor-Gadbois Centre, days pass without ever being the same.

Next to a 94-year-old man who is savoring his last family gathering in the courtyard, comfortably placed between his pillows while everyone raises a toast to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies, surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything
"For six months, there have always been three to five beds occupied by people under 45 years old with cancer," Dr. Christiane Martel is concerned.
53% of the patients admitted to the Victor-Gadboisarrivent center come from their home and 47% from the hospital.
Problem of access to palliative care

77% of Canadians simply do not have access to palliative care, that is, care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal phase of their life, whether at home, in the hospital, or in a care center.
And several organizations, such as the Victor-Gadbois Centre and the Palliative Care at Home Society of Grand Montréal, specialize almost exclusively in the care of cancer patients.
It is precisely that large relative lack of healthcare in Quebec that makes many doctors specializing in palliative care fear the adoption of a law regulating euthanasia and assisted suicide.
Since October, a manifesto signed by leading figures in palliative care, such as Dr. Balfour Mount and Dr. Bernard Lapointe, is circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.

According to Dr. Christiane Martel, the healthcare system of Quebec is not competent enough to ensure that anyone has the right to quality palliative care before the procedure is accepted for euthanasia.
"Recently," he says, "I have seen a patient spend 14 days in the Emergency Department suffering great pain without anything being done to relieve her."
"I fear that patients want to die simply because they are not receiving adequate care."
And in parallel, many oncologists stubbornly stick with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's chances of survival were already at their lowest when she left an exhausting chemotherapy treatment.
"When I told my oncologist that I wanted to stop treatment, she said that she was very sorry that I wanted to stop fighting," he reports.

Indeed, the PSA test sometimes produces erroneous results, with false negatives or even false positives, leading to unnecessary medical interventions.

We have consulted two experts.

I therefore recommend the test from the age of 50, or from the age of 40 if your father has had prostate cancer.
Black men have a higher risk index.

There are aggressive cancers and other cancers that are indolent.

I recommend that the test be done in any case.

Prevent the disease

Many others remain totally inexplicable.

A hopeful fact: 10 years after quitting smoking, the risk of dying from cancer is reduced by half.
The peso
According to the SCC, fatness and obesity also contribute to the development of the disease.
They increase the risks of breast cancer, colon and rectal cancer, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer, and uterine cancer.
"Studies show that regular physical activity throughout life protects against breast cancer," they add.
The food
The body also recommends limiting the consumption of red meats.
In large amounts, they increase the risk of developing colorectal cancer.
Sausage products should also be avoided.
The preservation of meat for smoking, drying, or salting may lead to the formation of carcinogenic substances.
"They can damage the body's cells and lead to the development of cancer," they explain to us.

In recent years, several scientists have studied the links between the complex vitamins and cancer.

While in one of them a decrease in the risk of prostate cancer was observed, in the other, what was observed was rather an increase.

According to the website The Particle Adventure from the Berkeley Laboratories, which, by the way, is excellent, bosons are divided into two groups: mesons, about which we will not speak here, and the "force particles," through which the great forces of nature are propagated and with which the Higgs boson would
These bosons, it should be emphasized here, are not the exotic creatures that we might believe.
In fact, if you manage to read this chronicle, it's thanks to an extraordinarily banal boson: the photon or the "light particle" that acts as a "messenger" of the electromagnetic force.
Indeed, when a charged particle accelerates or changes direction, it "disturbs" the electromagnetic field in that immediate vicinity; a bit like when we throw a stone into a pond.
In this "disorder" arises an electromagnetic wave (of light, of infrared, of ultraviolet, etc.), and this wave is nothing else but a photon; that is, one of the bosons "carriers of force".
More stable field
The same thing happens with the Higgs boson, with the difference that it is another field, the Higgs field, which needs to be "disordered" for this boson to appear.

Now, the Higgs field is much more stable than the electromagnetic field. To activate it, you need to reach extremely high energies, a bit like an ice pond where only a heavy rock could slide across the surface.
Therefore, an immense particle accelerator like the CERN one (the Large Hadron Collider is a 27 km circumference ring!) is needed to reach such energy levels.
The analogy with the electromagnetic field is a new tool that explains the relationship between the Higgs and mass.
In fact, not all particles or materials interact with the electromagnetic field.
Some, like the imams, do it, but others don't: a piece of paper, for example, will never remain stuck by itself to the door of a refrigerator.
Similarly, not all particles interact with the Higgs field: those that do have mass, while the rest (such as the photon, by the way) do not.
Now, what "can contribute" all those investigations, asks Madame Plamondon.
For science, this serves to verify the validity of the Standard Model (SM), and allows physicists to scrutinize the differences between observations and predictions of the SM.
On the other hand, many fervently hope that they are found, since the slightest difference could open a door to a "new physics" that would plug certain holes in the model.

This, one must say, still has enormous shortcomings, such as not proposing any explanation regarding gravity (oops!) or dark matter, which constitutes around 80% of the matter in the Universe (another oops!).
But we have not found such differences at CERN so far.
Repercussions

They foresaw scientific applications, but nothing more.

For example, the same Willard Boyle developed a light detector in 1969 during his research in optics.
Although it was absolutely not his original intention, this detector now serves as the "eye" for all the world's digital devices, which earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009.
That doesn't mean, of course, that the LHC activities necessarily want to transform our lives, but we never know...
Palliative care. The best way to die... | Le Devoir
In its Commission on Dying with Dignity, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of end-of-life.
The debate must be resumed soon as a bill is being prepared.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still much to be done.
Le Devoir has tried to get close to him.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. was living alone in his apartment in Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him a two-year reprieve.
"I had been given five years of life, but I've already lived seven," he recounts, a frail man lying in bed at the Victor-Gadbois palliative care center in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has caused him great trouble: a huge weakness that prevents him from going to the bathroom alone and even from eating by himself.
Sitting in front of a tempting lunch, he accepts resignedly that they help him eat.
Brave, he even smiles, talks to strangers who pay attention to him, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The bravery of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a remedy for that illness.
"Throughout our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, a psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois Centre.
Returning to one's childhood, for certain people, is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he notes.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients who enter the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses who surround them no longer offer "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., 89 years old, is to die "conscious and drowned".
But the illness has made him discover his children.
"I have some good children," he adds.
"I have no more wishes in this life," she says, before accepting that a mask will be placed on her to help her breathe.
And he is expecting, in the coming days, a final visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
They are palliative care that is given when nothing else can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have a palliative care bed for every 11,700 residents.
It's very little, since we know that we will all eventually die one day.
Here, life continues under the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the center.
Whether in terms of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual well-being.
The dying man is given mouth washings with brandy or Pepsi, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their blood sugar levels.
Death is part of the everyday.
Last night we served a beer to Mr. X, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both the patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
At the Victor-Gadbois Centre, days pass without ever being the same.

Next to a 94-year-old man who is savoring his last family gathering in the yard, comfortably placed between his pillows while everyone drinks to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies, surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything to survive
"For the past six months, there have always been three to five beds occupied by people under 45 with cancer," worries Dr. Christiane Martel.
53% of the patients admitted to the Victor-Gadboisarrivent center come from their home and 47% from the hospital.
Access to palliative care problem

77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, that is, to care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal phase of their life, whether at home, in a hospital, or in a care facility.
And several organizations, such as the Victor-Gadbois Centre and the Home Palliative Care Society of Grand Montréal, specialize almost exclusively in the care of cancer patients.
It is precisely that great relative lack of healthcare in Quebec that makes many doctors specializing in palliative care fear the adoption of a law regulating euthanasia and assisted suicide.

Since October, a manifesto signed by prominent figures in palliative care, such as Dr. Balfour Mount and Dr. Bernard Lapointe, has been circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.

According to Dr. Christiane Martel, the healthcare system in Quebec is not competent enough to ensure that anyone has the right to quality palliative care before proceeding with euthanasia is accepted.
"Recently," she says, "I have seen a patient spend 14 days in the Emergency Department suffering severe pain without anything being done to relieve her."
"I fear that patients want to die only because they are not receiving adequate care."
And in parallel, many oncologists persist with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's chances of survival were already at a low when she left an exhausting chemotherapy treatment.
"When I told my oncologist that I wanted to stop treatment, she said she was very sorry that I wanted to stop fighting," he reports.

A Republican strategy to block the re-election of Obama
The leaders of the Republican Party justified their policies as necessary to combat election fraud.

However, the Center for the study of the United States says that the last one is a myth and claims that election fraud is less common in the United States than the number of people who die from lightning strikes.
